bullets: Leverage feels free until the day it isn't — a principle that underscores how financial risk emerges not from the asset itself but from the method of financing it.
Most financial blow-ups stem not from poor asset selection but from improper financing — the same investment on margin can trigger forced liquidation during downturns.
An index fund held outright is patient capital; the same fund levered through margin becomes reactive and vulnerable to market stress.
The risk is not the investment’s return profile but the borrowing against it — margin amplifies downside exposure during volatility.
Forced selling on margin occurs precisely at the worst possible moment, turning a disciplined strategy into a reactive one.
Index investing benefits from long-term patience, but leverage distorts this by introducing short-term margin requirements.
A well-structured portfolio avoids risk by design — the real danger lies in the mechanics of financing, not the asset’s inherent value.
Understanding leverage is essential to preserving capital — the difference between a resilient and a failed position often lies in how it’s funded
